descriptors.definition: A demand-driven pull system focused on producing or procuring components exactly when required to systematically eliminate operational waste. It positively impacts product costs by reducing inventory buffers and streamlining production flows.
inclusion: Procuring raw materials for exact time usage
Producing finished goods based on actual customer demand
exclusion: Push systems relying on inventory stock buffers
nearby_distinctions: Unlike push systems that use stock buffers, JIT strictly responds to immediate demand.

descriptors.definition: An operational rollout plan structured into purchasing, production, and support phases to ensure raw materials arrive precisely when needed and work-in-process is minimized. It coordinates direct shop floor deliveries, supplier site evaluations, and accounting system modifications.
inclusion: Direct delivery to production floors
Supplier site visits by engineering staff
Shortening setup times
exclusion: Traditional long production runs with large inventory buffers
nearby_distinctions: Differs from general lean principles by explicitly sequencing purchasing, production, and support tasks.

descriptors.definition: Core operational characteristics that organize manufacturing into dedicated cells, employ multi-skilled workers, and apply total quality management to eliminate defects. These features drive down setup times, material-handling costs, and inventory levels.
inclusion: Grouping equipment into manufacturing cells
Preventive maintenance and defect elimination
exclusion: High variety of goods and unpredictable demand patterns
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from standard production by focusing on cellular layout and multi-skilling rather than functional specialization.

descriptors.concept_name: Impact of the JIT System on Costs and Prices
descriptors.definition: The systemic financial effect of JIT implementation resulting in reduced waste, lower overhead costs, and potential product price premiums due to enhanced quality. Warehouse space and associated facility costs decrease as inventory and material handling requirements drop.
inclusion: Reduction in storage space and warehouse staff overhead
Price adjustments based on high quality and delivery reliability
exclusion: Standard absorption costing adjustments unlinked to waste reduction
nearby_distinctions: Focuses on macro-level cost pool and pricing shifts rather than shop-floor sequencing mechanics.

descriptors.definition: An accounting simplification method that delays all inventory data entry until finished goods are completed, applying the bill of materials to calculate component usage. It eliminates transaction logs during intermediate stages but requires accurate production reporting and scrap tracking.
inclusion: Multiplying finished product counts by bill of materials quantities
Deducting components from beginning inventory in bulk
exclusion: Traditional sequential stage-by-stage inventory picking and logging
nearby_distinctions: Unlike standard costing which records transactions at each step, back-flushing delays all ledger entries until completion.

descriptors.definition: A continuous cost reduction system utilizing small, incremental improvements to achieve cost targets based on actual prior period results. It involves cross-functional teams repeatedly refining processes to maintain target profit margins against competitive price pressures.
inclusion: Elimination of waste in production and distribution processes
Establishing periodic cost reduction goals
exclusion: Radical one-off operational changes like business process re-engineering
nearby_distinctions: Differs from business process re-engineering by pursuing gradual incremental changes rather than radical overhauls.

descriptors.definition: A structured implementation mechanism involving setting cost reduction goals, determining gaps against actual costs, and executing plans through value analysis. It assumes continuous improvement conditions and assesses missing targets rather than calculating standard variances.
inclusion: Establishing a kaizen cost target
Formulating action plans via value analysis
nearby_distinctions: Unlike standard costing which analyzes variances under static conditions, Kaizen costing addresses performance gaps under continuous improvement.

descriptors.definition: The first phase of the 5S methodology that involves dividing workplace items into categories based on necessity and urgency of use. It utilizes visual management tools such as red and yellow tags to identify and eliminate obsolete, defective, or unnecessary items.
inclusion: Categorizing materials as not needed, needed later, or misplaced
Applying red and yellow identification tags
exclusion: Systemic arrangement or cleaning of retained items
nearby_distinctions: Focuses exclusively on separating necessary from unnecessary items before organizing or cleaning them.

descriptors.definition: The second phase of the 5S methodology that arranges necessary items into efficient, accessible locations following the principle that everything has a designated place. Its primary purpose is to eliminate search time and motion waste through visual management and structured placement.
inclusion: Placing frequently used components near workstations
Indexing and labelling items for rapid retrieval
exclusion: Discarding unneeded items or cleaning equipment surfaces
nearby_distinctions: Distinct from sorting by organizing retained items rather than discarding unneeded ones.

descriptors.definition: The third phase of the 5S methodology that mandates daily workstation cleanliness and comprehensive facility inspections to ensure safety and prevent accidents. Workers systematically clean and inspect all aspects of tools, machinery, and workspace surfaces.
inclusion: Daily workstation cleaning by workers
Multi-aspect inspection of machinery and tools
exclusion: Establishing formal organization-wide standard operating procedures
nearby_distinctions: Focuses on physical cleanliness and asset inspection rather than sorting or layout arrangement.

descriptors.definition: The fourth phase of the 5S methodology that integrates best workplace practices into organization-wide standard operating procedures. It maintains SMART standards to ensure that sorting, set-in-order, and shine activities become habitual routines.
inclusion: Creating formal procedures for orderliness
Embedding best practices into daily work habits
exclusion: Initial sorting or physical cleaning tasks
nearby_distinctions: Institutionalizes previous 5S steps into formal procedures rather than executing physical sorting or cleaning.

descriptors.definition: The final phase of the 5S methodology that maintains established standards through continuous monitoring, periodic audits, and employee engagement. It relies on assigned responsibilities, visual communication, and ongoing training to preserve lean disciplines.
inclusion: Periodic audits at all organizational levels
Continuous training and staff motivation
exclusion: Initial formulation of standard operating procedures
nearby_distinctions: Focuses on long-term compliance and monitoring rather than the initial creation of standards.
